Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers means jobs get picked up as soon as they land. A producer writes to Redis, SQS, or a Postgres table; a pool of long-lived workers pulls from it and processes each item. Latency is measured in seconds. You can scale by adding workers, and a poison message only blocks the one job that carries it, assuming you have retry limits and a dead-letter destination. What you pay for that is operational work. Workers are processes you have to keep alive, monitor for stalls, and drain cleanly on deploy. Ordering guarantees are weak unless you pay for them with partition keys or per-entity locks.

Scheduled batch runs are a cron entry and a script that queries for pending work. Nothing runs between invocations, so there is no idle process to babysit and no broker to operate. A batch can hold a transaction across the whole set, which makes idempotency and reconciliation much easier to reason about. The tradeoff is latency equal to the interval, plus thundering-herd load when the run starts.

Pick the queue when a user is waiting on the result, or when arrival rate is spiky and unbounded. Pick batch when the work is periodic anyway (nightly invoices, daily digests), when downstream systems have rate limits you'd rather manage in one place, or when your team is small enough that one less service matters.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

Failure is where the two diverge most sharply. In a queue, a failed job is a message that goes back on the queue with an incremented attempt count. The worker catches the exception, the broker redelivers after a backoff, and after some number of tries the message lands in a dead-letter queue where it sits until a human looks at it. Everything else keeps flowing. The cost is that partial work may already be committed: if the job charged a card and then failed writing the receipt, the retry charges the card again unless you built an idempotency key. In a batch run, a failure usually means one of two things. Either the script wraps the set in a transaction and the whole run rolls back, so nothing is half-done but nothing is done at all and you wait for the next window; or it processes row by row, logs the failures, and continues, which leaves you reading the log to find out what got skipped. Neither has automatic retry unless you write it. The failed rows stay in whatever pending state the query selects on, so the next scheduled run picks them up again by default, which is a real advantage — the retry mechanism is the query, and it costs you nothing to build.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a recommendation for a small team.

output: For a team of three to six engineers with no dedicated infrastructure person, start with scheduled batch runs against a Postgres table. A cron entry and a query that selects pending rows gives you retry, visibility, and a clear audit trail without a broker, a worker fleet, or a deploy story for long-lived processes. Run it every minute if you need lower latency; a one-minute cron plus `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` covers most workloads people reach for a queue to solve. Move to a real queue when you hit a specific wall: a user staring at a spinner waiting on the job, a burst that a single run cannot finish before the next one starts, or work that needs to fan out across more machines than one cron host has cores. Those are observable conditions, not guesses, and you will know when you hit them. Adopting SQS or a Redis-backed worker pool on day one buys latency you do not need yet and costs you a component that pages someone at 3am.
